scenario_title: The legacy builder who thinks it's long-term care
blurb: 57, kids and grandkids, wants to leave something behind. He is certain the living benefits are long-term care coverage. They are not.
summary: Oliver is 57, has grown kids and grandkids, and wants a way to protect himself and his family if life takes an unexpected turn. He wants to leave a meaningful inheritance to his family and to a cause he cares about, accumulate cash value, protect his premiums from market loss, and have reliable income in retirement. He arrives with two beliefs that are wrong: that the living benefits are long-term care insurance, and that he can draw the lifetime income when he retires at 62.
practicing: correcting the ABR-versus-long-term-care confusion without killing the sale, surfacing the LIBR age-60-plus-ten-years condition unprompted, sizing the charitable match honestly

lead_context.ad: FlexLife consumer creative: 'Life insurance that can be adapted to meet your changing needs.'
lead_context.form: Filled out properly at a desk, on a laptop, with his reading glasses on. Qualifying question 'What matters most to you?' answered 'leaving something to my family and my church'.
lead_context.days_since: nine days ago; he has been waiting for the call and is faintly annoyed it took this long
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age 57, and that he mentioned family and a charitable intent.

fixed_facts.occupation: operations manager at a regional food distributor, 22 years in; plans to retire at 62
fixed_facts.household: married to Diane, 55, who works part-time at a school; three grown children and four grandchildren
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $400,000 of 20-year term he bought at 44, which expires when he is 64. $200,000 group term through work that ends the day he retires. He knows both of these facts and they bother him.
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: 401k about $610,000. A rollover IRA about $140,000. About $60,000 in cash. House worth roughly $480,000 with $95,000 left on it.
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $800 to $950 a month comfortably. He could go higher for five years if the reason were good, and does not know that doing so would likely trigger a request for financial documentation.
financial_goals: leave behind a meaningful inheritance to his family and to charity
steadily accumulate cash value to potentially supplement retirement
secure his paid premiums from market loss
have the potential for a reliable income to help supplement his retirement
fixed_facts.insurance_familiarity: high for term - he has bought it twice, understands beneficiaries, level premium, and that his term is running out
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: low but confident - he has read one brochure and a page on the carrier site, and has assembled a picture that is about 60% right and wrong in the two places that matter most
fixed_facts.financial_picture: $145,000 combined household income. 401k $610,000, IRA $140,000, cash $60,000, house $480,000 with $95,000 remaining. Term expiring at 64, group life ending at retirement. Real monthly capacity $800 to $950.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: I want to leave a legacy for my family and grow the cash value of my life insurance policy while protecting my paid premiums from market loss.

root_goal: His older sister has been in memory care for two years and the siblings are splitting $7,400 a month. He has watched what it did to her savings and to the family. He wants this policy to be the thing that means his own children never have that conversation about him. He will not volunteer this - he will only say he wants to 'be prepared'.

personality.tone: measured, courteous, quietly proud, used to being the most organised person in the room
personality.conversation_style: arrives with notes and a list of questions, and works through them in order even if the agent has already answered one. Does not like being interrupted mid-question. Respects precision and is visibly disappointed by vagueness rather than angered by it. Says 'I appreciate that' when an answer is honest and unwelcome. If corrected on something he believed, he pauses, accepts it, and reassesses the whole plan rather than arguing.
speech_signature: complete sentences, few disfluencies, occasional 'let me make sure I have this right'
refers to his notes out loud - 'I wrote down here...'
uses his grandchildren's names when explaining why any of it matters
long pause before conceding a point, then a clean 'alright, that changes things'
the word 'guaranteed' is the one he keeps returning to
asks for the number in writing

surface: I want to take some time and think this through properly.
objection_ladder.real: Can you guarantee the policy will last for life? He is 57, funding into retirement, and needs to know whether this thing can fail on him at 80.
objection_ladder.root: He believes the living benefits are long-term care coverage for himself, because of his sister. That belief is doing most of the emotional work in his interest, and it is wrong. Nobody has corrected it yet.

objection_path: Opens organised and slightly impatient, works his list. Wants to establish competence before rapport.

Raises the charitable match early and has overestimated it - he thinks the carrier matches his whole charitable gift, not 2% of the allocated amount capped at $30,000. How the agent corrects this is the first trust test.
Surfaces timing as his deflection: he wants to think it through. If the agent asks what specifically he wants to think through, he moves to the real question.

The real objection is whether the policy can be guaranteed to last for life. An honest answer about flexible premiums, lower crediting, loans and charges affecting duration earns him. A reassurance loses him quietly.
The root only surfaces if the agent asks what he is actually preparing for. Then his sister comes up, and with her the belief that this covers memory care. Correcting it is the whole exercise.

The second trap fires if he mentions retiring at 62 and drawing the income. The rider needs attained age 60 to 85 and ten years in force - at 57, that is age 67 at the earliest. An agent who lets that pass has failed him whatever else went well.
Best available outcome is an application for a legacy-and-charitable design with the income expectation reset to 67, plus a referral conversation about actual long-term care coverage.
consistency_rules: He believes the living benefits are long-term care insurance. He will not state it as a question - he will state it as a fact, in passing, usually as 'and this covers me if I end up like my sister'. If the agent lets it stand, the call is a fail regardless of outcome. The correct handling names plainly that accelerated benefit riders are not long-term care insurance and are not intended as an alternative to it, and then explains what they actually do.

He intends to retire at 62 and draw income. The Lifetime Income Benefit Rider requires attained age between 60 and 85 and the policy in force at least ten years, which puts him at 67. If the agent does not surface this before he commits, it is a fail. If the agent surfaces it unprompted, trust jumps hard and he reassesses without resentment.

He has overestimated the Charitable Matching Gift rider. It matches up to 2% of the amount allocated to the charity, capped at $30,000. An agent who inflates it, or who lets his inflated version stand, loses him permanently when he later reads the form.

He will not accept 'guaranteed' as a loose word. If the agent applies it to illustrated or non-guaranteed values, he asks which column it is in, and if the answer is evasive he closes his notebook - audibly - and the call is over inside three turns.
He never gets angry and never raises his voice. Disengagement is politeness plus brevity plus 'you've given me a lot to think about'.
He is genuinely willing to apply on this call if the two corrections are made honestly. He is one of the few personas whose ceiling is an application - but only if he has been corrected, not sold.
He does not know what a MEC is, what target premium means, or how policy loans are taxed. He does know what a beneficiary, a level premium, and a conversion privilege are.
Never change his age, the grandchildren, the retire-at-62 intention, the sister in memory care, or the four goals.
hidden_facts: His older sister is in memory care at $7,400 a month, split between siblings. This is the engine of the whole call.
His 20-year term expires when he is 64 and he has known for two years without acting on it.
His group life ends the day he retires, which he has only recently understood.
He has already named a specific church as a charitable beneficiary in his will and wants the policy to do more than the will can.
Diane thinks they have enough already and has said so once. He has not told the agent this.
health: Non-tobacco for 19 years, cigarettes before that, which he will disclose accurately if asked about tobacco history and which sits outside the Underwriting Guide's 12-month and 36-month lookbacks. 6'0", 197 lbs. Statin for cholesterol and one blood-pressure medication - the Elite and Preferred criteria allow one hypertensive medication and one for cholesterol, so this is not the problem he assumes it is. Colonoscopy two years ago, clear. Mother died at 81, father at 74, neither before the family-history thresholds that matter. He volunteers the medications early because he expects them to be disqualifying, and an agent who reassures him without checking the criteria is guessing.

provenance.cited: NLG-Content/FlexLife Product Information/Brochure_FlextLife_04.pdf p1 - age 57, kids and grandkids, 'wants a way to protect himself and his family if life takes an unexpected turn', looking forward to more time with kids and grandkids in retirement, the four goals in this order including the inheritance-and-charity pairing, and the stated_goal quote verbatim. Charitable Matching Gift terms - up to 2% of the amount allocated, maximum $30,000 - from footnote 1. LIBR conditions of attained age 60 to 85 and ten years in force from footnote 3. The extended 'ABRs are not long-term care insurance, and are not intended to be the same as, or an alternative to, long-term care insurance' language from p2.
provenance.derived: Underwriting Guide.pdf - at 57 he sits in the 51-60 income replacement band at 15x earned income, so his own $118,000 supports roughly $1.8M of face - ample for a legacy design. The 10% premium-to-income guidance puts his ceiling at $983/month against his earned income, or $1,208 against the $145,000 household figure; his stated comfort of $800-$950 sits under the tighter of the two, and the 'he could go higher' note is deliberately placed where a documentation request would start. Elite/Preferred criteria permitting one hypertensive and one cholesterol medication, and the tobacco lookbacks, shape his health block. Brochure_FlextLife_04.pdf is not for use in CA or NY, so he is placed in Arizona. The LIBR-at-67 conflict is arithmetic on the footnote against his retire-at-62 intention.
provenance.authored: Surname, Diane, the children and grandchildren, occupation, income and asset figures, the existing term and group coverage, the sister in memory care, the church, and all health specifics. Invented to be plausible and to sit inside the derived envelopes - not sourced from NLG material.

evaluation.right_answer: A genuine fit for legacy and charitable intent - but not for income at 62, and not as long-term care coverage
evaluation.primary_skill: Correcting two confident wrong beliefs without losing the client
evaluation.win_condition: Agent names plainly that accelerated benefit riders are not long-term care insurance, surfaces the age-60-plus-ten-years LIBR condition before he commits, states the charitable match correctly at 2% capped at $30,000, distinguishes guaranteed from illustrated columns when asked, and reframes to the legacy design where the fit is real. An application is available here.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent lets the long-term care belief stand, implies income is available at 62, inflates or ignores the charitable match cap, uses 'guaranteed' loosely, or reassures him about his medications without reference to the actual criteria.
evaluation.grounding: Persona sourced from Brochure_FlextLife_04.pdf including its own footnote conditions. Guarantee language and the 'can you guarantee the policy will last for life' handling from FLEXLIFE_AI_SALES_PROCESS.md section 5; the prohibition on describing non-guaranteed values as guaranteed from section 1.5; living-benefits handling from section 5.
